Currently, `--kv-cache-dtype auto` falls back to `model_config.dtype` instead of using the checkpoint's specified FP8 quantization. Additionally, explicitly overriding with `--kv-cache-dtype bfloat16` raises an error. ## Expected Behavior **For models that specify `kv_cache_quant_algo` in checkpoint:** | `--kv-cache-dtype` | Expected behavior | Current behavior | Status | |---|---|---|---| | `auto` | Use checkpoint's specified dtype (e.g., FP8) | Falls back to `model_config.dtype` | ❌ Bug | | `fp8` | Use FP8 | Uses FP8 | ✅ Works | | `bfloat16` | Use BF16 (override checkpoint) | Raises error | ❌ Bug | | *(not specified)* | Use checkpoint's specified dtype | Uses checkpoint's specified dtype | ✅ Works | ### For models that DON'T specify `kv_cache_quant_algo` | `--kv-cache-dtype` | Expected behavior | Current behavior | Status | |---|---|---|---| | `auto` | Use `model_config.dtype` | Uses `model_config.dtype` | ✅ Works | | `fp8` | Use FP8 | Uses FP8 | ✅ Works | | `bfloat16` | Use BF16 | *(untested)* | ❓ Unknown | | *(not specified)* | Use `model_config.dtype` | Uses `model_config.dtype` | ✅ Works Observed error when bfloat16 is specified: ``` (EngineCore_DP0 pid=57748) File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/vllm/v1/attention/backends/flashinfer.py", line 1341, in forward (EngineCore_DP0 pid=57748) torch.ops._C_cache_ops.reshape_and_cache_flash( (EngineCore_DP0 pid=57748) File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/torch/_ops.py", line 1209, in __call__ (EngineCore_DP0 pid=57748) return self._op(*args, **kwargs) (EngineCore_DP0 pid=57748) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ (EngineCore_DP0 pid=57748) RuntimeError: Unsupported data type of kv cache: bfloat16 [rank0]:[W217 21:11:54.961492204 ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp:1553] Warning: WARNING: destroy_process_group() was not called before program exit, which can leak resources.     "content": "{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"pull_request\",\n  \"author\": \"alvinttang\",\n  \"body\": \"## Summary\\n\\nFixes #34752\\n\\nWhen a model checkpoint specifies `kv_cache_quant_algo` (e.g., FP8 via modelopt quantization config), `--kv-cache-dtype auto` should auto-detect and use that dtype instead of falling back to `model_config.dtype`.\\n\\n### Changes\\n\\n- **`vllm/config/vllm.py`**: Added KV cache dtype resolution logic at the end of `try_verify_and_update_config()`. When `cache_dtype` is `\\\"auto\\\"`, it calls the existing `resolve_kv_cache_dtype_string()` helper from `torch_utils.py` to check if the model's quantization config specifies a `kv_cache_quant_algo`. If found (e.g., FP8), it updates `cache_dtype` accordingly and logs the auto-detected value.\\n\\n- **`tests/test_config.py`**: Added `test_resolve_kv_cache_dtype_string` unit test covering:\\n  - No quantization config -> stays \\\"auto\\\"\\n  - modelopt with FP8 `kv_cache_quant_algo` -> resolves to \\\"fp8_e4m3\\\"\\n  - modelopt without `kv_cache_quant_algo` -> stays \\\"auto\\\"\\n  - Non-auto values pass through unchanged\\n  - Missing `hf_config` -> stays \\\"auto\\\"\\n\\n### Resolution Logic\\n\\nThe existing `resolve_kv_cache_dtype_string` and `get_kv_cache_quant_algo_string` helpers in `torch_utils.py` already handle the mapping from modelopt's `kv_cache_quant_algo` to vLLM's cache dtype strings. This PR simply wires them into the config initialization flow so that auto-detection happens automatically.\\n\\n| `--kv-cache-dtype` | Model has `kv_cache_quant_algo=FP8` | Result |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| `auto` (default) | Yes | `fp8_e4m3` (auto-detected) |\\n| `auto` (default) | No | `auto` (uses model dtype) |\\n| `fp8` | Yes/No | `fp8` (explicit override) |\\n| `bfloat16` | Yes/No | `bfloat16` (explicit override) |\\n\\n## Test plan\\n\\n- [ ] `pytest tests/test_config.py::test_resolve_kv_cache_dtype_string -v`\\n- [ ] Verify with a model that has `kv_cache_quant_algo` set (e.g., `nvidia/Qwen3-30B-A3B-NVFP4`) that auto-detection works\\n- [ ] Verify that explicit `--kv-cache-dtype` values still override the auto-detection\\n\\n\\ud83e\\udd16 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)\",\n  \"changed_files\": [\n    \"tests/test_config.py (+42, -0, MODIFIED)\",\n    \"vllm/config/vllm.py (+15, -0, MODIFIED)\"\n  ],\n  \"closed_at\": \"2026-03-16T10:17:22Z\",\n  \"comments_count\": 0,\n  \"commit_summaries\": [\n    \"2026-03-14T07:03:47Z fdcebde91f13: fix: resolve kv_cache_dtype='auto' from checkpoint kv_cache_quant_algo\",\n    \"2026-03-14T07:03:47Z 52d2022172ab: test: add unit test for resolve_kv_cache_dtype_string\",\n    \"2026-03-14T07:03:47Z 7ae5dc9180dc: style: fix pre-commit formatting in vllm/config/vllm.py\"\n  ],\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\",\n    \"conversation\",\n    \"reviews\",\n    \"commit_summaries\",\n    \"changed_files\",\n    \"timeline\"\n  ],\n  \"conversation\": [],\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-03-14T04:06:49Z\",\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"gh_fb6cb2d26b08d0e2362bdc1df907d650\",\n  \"draft\": false,\n  \"labels\": [],\n  \"merged_at\": \"\",\n  \"milestone\": \"\",\n  \"number\": 37034,\n  \"owner\": \"vllm-project\",\n  \"provenance\": [\n    \"GitHub REST and GraphQL API; repository=vllm-project/vllm\",\n    \"cutoff=2026-07-27T23:59:59Z\",\n    \"body_status=rest-object-before-cutoff\",\n    \"changed_files_status=available\"\n  ],\n  \"repo\": \"vllm\",\n  \"repository\": \"vllm-project/vllm\",\n  \"review_comments_count\": 0,\n  \"reviews\": [\n    \"2026-03-14T04:09:40Z gemini-code-assist [COMMENTED]: ## Code Review\\n\\nThis pull request correctly implements the logic to auto-detect `kv_cache_dtype` from the model's quantization configuration when it is set to 'auto'. The changes in `vllm/config/vllm.py` are clean and placed appropriately within the configuration initialization flow. The accompanying unit tests in `tests/test_config.py` are comprehensive and effectively validate the new behavior across various scenarios. The implementation is solid and I have no major concerns.\",\n    \"2026-03-14T07:03:59Z alvinttang [COMMENTED]: ## Code Review: Resolve kv_cache_dtype='auto' from Checkpoint\\n\\nGood UX improvement \\u2014 users with modelopt FP8-quantized checkpoints that include `kv_cache_quant_algo` no longer need to manually specify `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`.\\n\\n### Concerns\\n\\n**1. The `resolve_kv_cache_dtype_string` function is not in this diff**\\nThis PR calls `resolve_kv_cache_dtype_string` from `vllm.utils.torch_utils`, but the function implementation is not included in the changeset. If this function does not yet exist on `main`, this PR will fail at import time. If it does exist, could you confirm which commit introduced it? It would be helpful to see its implementation to verify correctness of the mapping (e.g., does it handle `kv_cache_quant_algo: \\\"FP8\\\"` -> `\\\"fp8_e4m3\\\"` correctly? What about INT8 or other quantization algorithms?).\\n\\n**2. `object.__setattr__` bypasses frozen dataclass validation**\\n```python\\nobject.__setattr__(self.cache_config, \\\"cache_dtype\\\", resolved)\\n```\\nThis is necessary because `CacheConfig` is likely a frozen dataclass, but it bypasses any `__post_init__` validation. If `CacheConfig.__post_init__` performs consistency checks (e.g., verifying cache_dtype against other fields like `num_gpu_blocks_override`), those checks are silently skipped. Consider whether calling a dedicated setter or re-running validation after mutation would be safer.\\n\\n**3. Only `modelopt` with `FP8` is tested**\\nThe tests cover the happy path well, but consider:\\n- What happens with `kv_cache_quant_algo: \\\"INT8\\\"`? Should that resolve to `\\\"int8\\\"` or remain `\\\"auto\\\"`?\\n- What about non-modelopt quantization methods (e.g., GPTQ, AWQ) that might also have a `kv_cache_quant_algo` field?\\n- What if `quantization_config` is an object (some HF configs use dataclass-like objects rather than dicts)?\\n\\n**4. Timing of resolution**\\nThe resolution happens in `try_verify_and_update_config()`. Is this early enough? If any downstream code reads `cache_config.cache_dtype` before `try_verify_and_update_config()` is called, it would still see `\\\"auto\\\"` and potentially make wrong decisions. It would be good to verify no code path reads `cache_dtype` before this point.\\n\\n**5. Missing test for `hf_config` without `quantization_config` attribute**\\nTest case 5 sets `hf_config = None`, but a more realistic edge case is `hf_config` exists but has no `quantization_config` attribute at all (i.e., `hasattr(hf_config, 'quantization_config')` returns False). MagicMock auto-creates attributes, so `model_config.hf_config.quantization_config = None` doesn't test the \\\"attribute missing\\\" case.\\n\\n### Minor\\n- The info-level log message is a nice touch \\u2014 users will see exactly what happened during startup.\\n- Good that non-`\\\"auto\\\"` values pass through unchanged (test case 4).\\n\\nOverall the approach is sound. The main risk is the missing function implementation and the potential for `object.__setattr__` to bypass validation.\"\n  ],\n  \"source\": \"github_public\",\n  \"state\": \"closed\",\n  \"state_at_cutoff\": \"closed\",\n  \"timeline\": [],\n  \"title\": \"fix: resolve kv_cache_dtype='auto' from checkpoint kv_cache_quant_algo\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"updated_at\": \"2026-03-16T10:17:22Z\",\n  \"url\": \"https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/37034\"\n}\n",

document.title: fix: resolve kv_cache_dtype='auto' from checkpoint kv_cache_quant_algo
document.content:
{
  "artifact_type": "pull_request",
  "author": "alvinttang",
  "body": "## Summary

Fixes #34752

When a model checkpoint specifies `kv_cache_quant_algo` (e.g., FP8 via modelopt quantization config), `--kv-cache-dtype auto` should auto-detect and use that dtype instead of falling back to `model_config.dtype`.

### Changes

- **`vllm/config/vllm.py`**: Added KV cache dtype resolution logic at the end of `try_verify_and_update_config()`. When `cache_dtype` is `"auto"`, it calls the existing `resolve_kv_cache_dtype_string()` helper from `torch_utils.py` to check if the model's quantization config specifies a `kv_cache_quant_algo`. If found (e.g., FP8), it updates `cache_dtype` accordingly and logs the auto-detected value.

- **`tests/test_config.py`**: Added `test_resolve_kv_cache_dtype_string` unit test covering:
  - No quantization config -> stays "auto"
  - modelopt with FP8 `kv_cache_quant_algo` -> resolves to "fp8_e4m3"
  - modelopt without `kv_cache_quant_algo` -> stays "auto"
  - Non-auto values pass through unchanged
  - Missing `hf_config` -> stays "auto"

### Resolution Logic

The existing `resolve_kv_cache_dtype_string` and `get_kv_cache_quant_algo_string` helpers in `torch_utils.py` already handle the mapping from modelopt's `kv_cache_quant_algo` to vLLM's cache dtype strings. This PR simply wires them into the config initialization flow so that auto-detection happens automatically.

| `--kv-cache-dtype` | Model has `kv_cache_quant_algo=FP8` | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `auto` (default) | Yes | `fp8_e4m3` (auto-detected) |
| `auto` (default) | No | `auto` (uses model dtype) |
| `fp8` | Yes/No | `fp8` (explicit override) |
| `bfloat16` | Yes/No | `bfloat16` (explicit override) |

## Test plan

- [ ] `pytest tests/test_config.py::test_resolve_kv_cache_dtype_string -v`
- [ ] Verify with a model that has `kv_cache_quant_algo` set (e.g., `nvidia/Qwen3-30B-A3B-NVFP4`) that auto-detection works
- [ ] Verify that explicit `--kv-cache-dtype` values still override the auto-detection

Each subscriber gets updates via streaming API (gRPC) and a fallback REST listing endpoint.\\n\\n2) Lightweight region caches (service discovery layer)\\n- Each serving runtime region runs an in-memory cache (node-catalog) that subscribes to node-registry.\\n- Cache TTL for soft entries configurable; hard TTL for offline nodes to avoid immediate eviction if transient networking flaps.\\n- Edge policy: router prefers same-region nodes, but will route cross-region if compatibility/capacity requires it. Caching ensures routing decisions don\\u2019t require control-plane roundtrips at request time.\\n\\nLabel schema (canonical keys and examples)\\n- Naming convention: redwood/<category>/<property> (lowercase, hyphen-separated). Keep keys short but unambiguous.\\n- Required fields (always present):\\n  - redwood/hardware/gpu_count: integer (0,1,2...)\\n  - redwood/hardware/gpu_model: short string (a100-80c, h100-80, t4-16gb)\\n  - redwood/hardware/gpu_driver: semantic (nvidia-535.XX)\\n  - redwood/hardware/mig_capable: boolean (true/false)\\n  - redwood/region: region-id (e.g., us-west1)\\n  - redwood/instance-type: cloud instance (e.g., g4dn.xlarge) or private flavor id\\n- Optional capability flags:\\n  - redwood/runtime/quantized-ops: list of quantization formats supported (q4_0,q4_1,int8)\\n  - redwood/runtime/cpu_isa: avx512/avx2/armv8\\n  - redwood/network/bandwidth_gbps: integer\\n- Dynamic health metadata (not a kube label; surfaced in registry stream with timestamps):\\n  - health/score: 0..100 (higher is better)\\n  - health/last-heartbeat: ISO8601 timestamp\\n  - health/tail-latency-ms-p90: integer\\n  - health/recent-failures: windowed count (last 10m)\\n\\nWhy separate static labels and dynamic health signals?\\n- Labels should be slow-changing and cacheable. Health is high-cardinality and high-frequency; putting it in a label store causes chattiness. The registry exposes both but different transport modes: labels via listing/snapshot; health via push streaming.\\n\\nGPU compatibility discovery\\n- Node agent (already deployed) runs a lightweight probe at boot and daily: records GPU PCI ids, driver version, cuda toolkit version, mig partitions, and a small kernel of supported ops (via a micro-benchmark).\\n- Agent writes to a local file and publishes a signed message to node-registry; we avoid writing untrusted raw driver strings into public logs for privacy in Private deployments.\\n- Compatibility matrix: the registry maintains a small matrix for model families -> required features (min driver, quantization support, required memory per tensor). Router queries this to map a model variant to suitable nodes.\\n- Fallback behavior: if a node advertises an older driver but passes runtime smoke-tests, we allow routing with a strictness score reduction (e.g., 90 -> 75). This prevents brittle behavior during rolling driver upgrades.\\n\\nHealth signals design and scoring\\n- Health is a composite score derived from: heartbeat recency (30%), GPU error counters (25%), scheduling queue length (20%), tail latency (15%), thermals/clock throttling indicator (10%). We weight and expose the raw contributors for auditability.\\n- Nodes with score < 40 are marked in the registry as degraded; routers apply a soft-penalty multiplier to routing cost instead of immediate exclusion.\\n- Escalation: repeated degradation events (3 in 15m) generate an incident signal to SRE and trigger an autoscaler probe to shift load.\\n- Circuit breaker: if a node's recent failure rate for the last 1m exceeds threshold, it is temporarily tainted for scheduler to avoid new allocations; taint cleared after cooldown + successful smoke test.\\n\\nRouting policy integration points\\n- Router uses a configurable cost function: cost = base_latency_estimate * health_multiplier * compatibility_penalty * region_penalty * utilization_penalty. Teams can define per-model policies (latency-first, cost-first, compatibility-must).\\n- Example policies:\\n  - low-latency: region_penalty = 100 for cross-region, compatibility_penalty = 0 for exact-match, health_multiplier = linear based on score\\n  - cheap-batch: prefer nodes with high utilization and quantized ops support; tolerate older drivers (lower compatibility score)\\n\\nConsistency and upgrade considerations\\n- Migration pattern for changing label keys:\\n  1) Introduce new key alongside old (dual-write in registry for a deprecation window).\\n  2) Emit deprecation telemetry on consumers still reading old key.\\n  3) After window, remove old key.\\n- Versioning: label schema has a semantic version number published from node-registry (schema_v=2). Consumers subscribe to schema changes.\\n\\nOperational playbook (practical checklist)\\n- Onboard new region:\\n  1) bootstrap node-registry with a snapshot seed (export from existing region).\\n  2) verify agent signing keys and default probe cadence.\\n  3) validate mapping for cloud tags -> canonical keys.\\n  4) run smoke: deploy canary jobs that request specific GPU models and verify routing.\\n- Respond to GPU driver incident:\\n  1) Use registry to identify nodes with matching driver versions.\\n  2) If fail patterns seen, set compatibility_penalty high for affected model families.\\n  3) Schedule rolling driver upgrade via release-engineering with staged canaries.\\n\\nData retention and telemetry\\n- Keep change-log events for 90 days to support debugging of rollout regressions. Aggregated health metrics retained 365d for capacity planning.\\n- Telemetry to include: label-change events, health-score timeline per node, routing decision traces referencing node id and cost factors.\\n\\nEdge cases and open questions\\n- Private/on-prem networks: how do we safely sign and accept node-reported GPU metadata from customer-managed agents? Proposal: mutual TLS with customer-provided CA and encrypted persistence in Private mode.\\n- Multi-tenant nodes (sharing GPUs across tenants): need tenant-aware capacity fields and isolation flags (schedule only if tenant matches).\\n- Distributed caches stale window: what TTL keeps routing stable during regional partitions? We propose 30s soft TTL with exponential backoff for refresh attempts.\\n\\nNext steps and action items\\n- Implement schema_v2 in node-registry (owner: Marco, ETA: 2 wks).\\n- Add health score contributors to node-agent (owner: Samira, ETA: 3 wks).\\n- Router integration spike to consume health stream and compute cost function (owner: Ethan, ETA: 2 wks).\\n- Validation harness: create a small testbed that simulates driver upgrades and heartbeats to validate scoring and routing behavior (owner: Aisha, ETA: 4 wks).\\n\\nAppendix: example entries\\n- Static snapshot example (registry list entry):\\n  id: node-az1-00012\\n  redwood/region: us-west1\\n  redwood/hardware/gpu_count: 8\\n  redwood/hardware/gpu_model: a100-80c\\n  redwood/hardware/gpu_driver: nvidia-535.54\\n  redwood/hardware/mig_capable: true\\n\\n- Health stream example (pushed event):\\n  id: node-az1-00012\\n  health/score: 72\\n  health/last-heartbeat: 2025-01-28T14:03:12Z\\n  health/tail-latency-ms-p90: 48\\n  health/recent-failures: 0\\n\\nNotes to reviewers:\\n- Focus feedback on the label naming conventions and health weightings \\u2014 both will affect consumer behavior heavily.\\n- Call out any compatibility checks we might have missed (e.g., driver microcode, BIOS/firmware flags).\\n\\nReferences:\\n- Related design: platform-engineering/node-fleet-registry-and-health-design.json (existing)\\n- GitHub PR for registry prototype: github:github.com/redwood-inference/platform-registry/pull/291\\n\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_6c5587faa14d49969531585fe1191c52\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Node metadata propagation and GPU compatibility guide\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/google_drive\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/platform-engineering/node-metadata-propagation-and-gpu-compatibility-guide.json\nConnector: google_drive\nWorkspace: shared_drives\nTeam: eng-platform-engineering\n\ngpu compatibility discovery - node agent ( already deployed ) runs a lightweight probe at boot and daily : records gpu pci ids, driver version, cuda toolkit version, mig partitions, and a small kernel of supported ops ( via a micro - benchmark ). - agent writes to a local file and publishes a signed message to node - registry ; we avoid writing untrusted raw driver strings into public logs for privacy in private deployments. - compatibility matrix : the registry maintains a small matrix for model families - > required features ( min driver, quantization support, required memory per tensor ). router queries this to map a model variant to suitable nodes. - fallback behavior : if a node advertises an older driver but passes runtime smoke - tests",

document.title: Node metadata propagation and GPU compatibility guide
document.content:
{
  "title": "Node metadata propagation and GPU compatibility guide",
  "owner": "Aisha Patel",
  "drive_area": "shared_drives",
  "path": "shared_drives/engineering/platform-engineering/node-metadata-propagation-and-gpu-compatibility-guide.json",
  "doc_type": "doc",
  "created_at": "2025-01-14",
  "last_modified": "2025-02-04",
  "collaborators": [
    "Marco Liu",
    "Samira Gomez",
    "Ethan Brooks"
  ],
  "team": "eng-platform-engineering",
  "status": "in_review",
  "tags": [
    "service-discovery",
    "node-labels",
    "gpu-compat",
    "health-signals",
    "multi-region"
  ],
  "linked_artifacts": [
    "confluence:PLAT-node-metadata-v2",
    "jira:PLAT-4782",
    "github:github.com/redwood-inference/platform-registry/pull/291"
  ],
  "content": "Purpose and scope:
This note captures an opinionated approach for node metadata propagation, label schema, GPU capability discovery, and health signal design for the platform control plane and service discovery layers. It focuses on implementation patterns we can standardize across multi-region clusters and across dedicated/private deployments.

Context and goals:
- Problem: teams need a reliable way to discover node capabilities (GPU model, memory, driver, MIG support), route requests by latency/cost/compatibility, and react to transient health issues without causing noisy failure cascades. Current inventory is fragmented (kube labels, cloud tags, Fleet DB) and we have divergent consumers (scheduler, autoscaler, runtime router).
- Goals:
  - Single source-of-truth for node capability metadata with clear sync semantics.
  - Stable label keys and a backwards-compatible upgrade path.
  - Fast health signal surface for routing decisions with scored health (not binary).
  - Lightweight per-region caches for low-latency service discovery.

High-level design:
1) Canonical node registry service (control-plane component)
- A small control-plane service (node-registry) lives in each control-plane region.
- It ingests: cloud provider tags/labels, kube node status, NVSM driver probes (via node agent), and CRDs from Private customers (when present).
- Normalization step: map provider-specific keys to our canonical schema (see Label schema).
- Persistent store: append-only change log in a regionally replicated DB (eventually consistent cross-region).
- Subscribers: routers (runtime), autoscaler, SRE tooling, console. Each subscriber gets updates via streaming API (gRPC) and a fallback REST listing endpoint.

2) Lightweight region caches (service discovery layer)
- Each serving runtime region runs an in-memory cache (node-catalog) that subscribes to node-registry.
- Cache TTL for soft entries configurable; hard TTL for offline nodes to avoid immediate eviction if transient networking flaps.
- Edge policy: router prefers same-region nodes, but will route cross-region if compatibility/capacity requires it. Caching ensures routing decisions don’t require control-plane roundtrips at request time.

Label schema (canonical keys and examples)
- Naming convention: redwood/<category>/<property> (lowercase, hyphen-separated). Keep keys short but unambiguous.
- Required fields (always present):
  - redwood/hardware/gpu_count: integer (0,1,2...)
  - redwood/hardware/gpu_model: short string (a100-80c, h100-80, t4-16gb)
  - redwood/hardware/gpu_driver: semantic (nvidia-535.XX)
  - redwood/hardware/mig_capable: boolean (true/false)
  - redwood/region: region-id (e.g., us-west1)
  - redwood/instance-type: cloud instance (e.g., g4dn.xlarge) or private flavor id
- Optional capability flags:
  - redwood/runtime/quantized-ops: list of quantization formats supported (q4_0,q4_1,int8)
  - redwood/runtime/cpu_isa: avx512/avx2/armv8
  - redwood/network/bandwidth_gbps: integer
- Dynamic health metadata (not a kube label; surfaced in registry stream with timestamps):
  - health/score: 0..100 (higher is better)
  - health/last-heartbeat: ISO8601 timestamp
  - health/tail-latency-ms-p90: integer
  - health/recent-failures: windowed count (last 10m)

Why separate static labels and dynamic health signals?
- Labels should be slow-changing and cacheable. Health is high-cardinality and high-frequency; putting it in a label store causes chattiness. The registry exposes both but different transport modes: labels via listing/snapshot; health via push streaming.

GPU compatibility discovery
- Node agent (already deployed) runs a lightweight probe at boot and daily: records GPU PCI ids, driver version, cuda toolkit version, mig partitions, and a small kernel of supported ops (via a micro-benchmark).
- Agent writes to a local file and publishes a signed message to node-registry; we avoid writing untrusted raw driver strings into public logs for privacy in Private deployments.
- Compatibility matrix: the registry maintains a small matrix for model families -> required features (min driver, quantization support, required memory per tensor). Router queries this to map a model variant to suitable nodes.
- Fallback behavior: if a node advertises an older driver but passes runtime smoke-tests, we allow routing with a strictness score reduction (e.g., 90 -> 75). This prevents brittle behavior during rolling driver upgrades.

Health signals design and scoring
- Health is a composite score derived from: heartbeat recency (30%), GPU error counters (25%), scheduling queue length (20%), tail latency (15%), thermals/clock throttling indicator (10%). We weight and expose the raw contributors for auditability.
- Nodes with score < 40 are marked in the registry as degraded; routers apply a soft-penalty multiplier to routing cost instead of immediate exclusion.
- Escalation: repeated degradation events (3 in 15m) generate an incident signal to SRE and trigger an autoscaler probe to shift load.
- Circuit breaker: if a node's recent failure rate for the last 1m exceeds threshold, it is temporarily tainted for scheduler to avoid new allocations; taint cleared after cooldown + successful smoke test.

Routing policy integration points
- Router uses a configurable cost function: cost = base_latency_estimate * health_multiplier * compatibility_penalty * region_penalty * utilization_penalty. Teams can define per-model policies (latency-first, cost-first, compatibility-must).
- Example policies:
  - low-latency: region_penalty = 100 for cross-region, compatibility_penalty = 0 for exact-match, health_multiplier = linear based on score
  - cheap-batch: prefer nodes with high utilization and quantized ops support; tolerate older drivers (lower compatibility score)

Consistency and upgrade considerations
- Migration pattern for changing label keys:
  1) Introduce new key alongside old (dual-write in registry for a deprecation window).
  2) Emit deprecation telemetry on consumers still reading old key.
  3) After window, remove old key.
- Versioning: label schema has a semantic version number published from node-registry (schema_v=2). Consumers subscribe to schema changes.

Operational playbook (practical checklist)
- Onboard new region:
  1) bootstrap node-registry with a snapshot seed (export from existing region).
  2) verify agent signing keys and default probe cadence.
  3) validate mapping for cloud tags -> canonical keys.
  4) run smoke: deploy canary jobs that request specific GPU models and verify routing.
- Respond to GPU driver incident:
  1) Use registry to identify nodes with matching driver versions.
  2) If fail patterns seen, set compatibility_penalty high for affected model families.
  3) Schedule rolling driver upgrade via release-engineering with staged canaries.

Data retention and telemetry
- Keep change-log events for 90 days to support debugging of rollout regressions. Aggregated health metrics retained 365d for capacity planning.
- Telemetry to include: label-change events, health-score timeline per node, routing decision traces referencing node id and cost factors.

Edge cases and open questions
- Private/on-prem networks: how do we safely sign and accept node-reported GPU metadata from customer-managed agents? Proposal: mutual TLS with customer-provided CA and encrypted persistence in Private mode.
- Multi-tenant nodes (sharing GPUs across tenants): need tenant-aware capacity fields and isolation flags (schedule only if tenant matches).
- Distributed caches stale window: what TTL keeps routing stable during regional partitions? We propose 30s soft TTL with exponential backoff for refresh attempts.

Next steps and action items
- Implement schema_v2 in node-registry (owner: Marco, ETA: 2 wks).
- Add health score contributors to node-agent (owner: Samira, ETA: 3 wks).
- Router integration spike to consume health stream and compute cost function (owner: Ethan, ETA: 2 wks).
- Validation harness: create a small testbed that simulates driver upgrades and heartbeats to validate scoring and routing behavior (owner: Aisha, ETA: 4 wks).

Appendix: example entries
- Static snapshot example (registry list entry):
  id: node-az1-00012
  redwood/region: us-west1
  redwood/hardware/gpu_count: 8
  redwood/hardware/gpu_model: a100-80c
  redwood/hardware/gpu_driver: nvidia-535.54
  redwood/hardware/mig_capable: true

- Health stream example (pushed event):
  id: node-az1-00012
  health/score: 72
  health/last-heartbeat: 2025-01-28T14:03:12Z
  health/tail-latency-ms-p90: 48
  health/recent-failures: 0

Notes to reviewers:
- Focus feedback on the label naming conventions and health weightings — both will affect consumer behavior heavily.
- Call out any compatibility checks we might have missed (e.g., driver microcode, BIOS/firmware flags).

References:
- Related design: platform-engineering/node-fleet-registry-and-health-design.json (existing)
- GitHub PR for registry prototype: github:github.com/redwood-inference/platform-registry/pull/291

{

    "id": "dsid_79aba7601ab24ca699516975ecd5dd86",

    "title": "Economizer Serving Recommendations Standard (Batching, Prefix Cache, Quantization)",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Economizer Serving Recommendations Standard (Batching, Prefix Cache, Quantization)\",\n  \"space\": \"eng-serving-runtime\",\n  \"author\": \"Priya Menon\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-03-10\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-05-12\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Carlos Rivera\",\n    \"Aisha Patel\",\n    \"Evan Zhang\",\n    \"Mina Al-Khalil\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"runtime\",\n    \"performance\",\n    \"cost\",\n    \"ml-serving\",\n    \"economizer\",\n    \"standards\",\n    \"rollouts\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"confluence://eng-serving-runtime/rollouts/canary-rollout-standard\",\n    \"confluence://eng-sre/observability/telemetry-retention-and-pii-scrubbing\",\n    \"confluence://eng-serving-runtime/caching/prefix-cache-architecture\",\n    \"confluence://eng-serving-runtime/model-registry/quantization-compatibility-matrix\"\n  ],\n  \"summary\": \"This standard defines how Redwood Inference uses Economizer to generate, review, and safely apply automated serving recommendations for batching, prefix caching, and quantization on a per-route and per-model basis. It establishes required guardrails (SLO impact thresholds, rollback, audit logging), telemetry requirements, and the operator workflow in Console/CLI.\",\n  \"body\": \"h1. Overview\\nEconomizer is Redwood Inference\\u2019s recommendation engine for serving configuration changes. It analyzes historical request traces plus live telemetry summaries to propose per-route and per-model adjustments that reduce token spend while keeping latency and error-rate within policy.\\n\\nEconomizer produces three classes of recommendations:\\n* *Batching* (e.g., target batch size range, max queue delay)\\n* *Prefix caching* (e.g., enablement, TTL and admission thresholds)\\n* *Quantization profiles* (e.g., FP16 baseline to INT8/FP8 where validated)\\n\\nThis page is the canonical standard for how recommendations are generated, surfaced, validated, and applied.\\n\\nh1. Scope\\nThis standard applies to:\\n* All production serving routes in Redwood Inference clusters\\n* Console-based recommendation preview and canary application flows\\n* CLI export used for audit/on-prem workflows\\n\\nOut of scope:\\n* Model quality evaluation methodology beyond the defined quantization gates (see related pages)\\n* Customer-facing product messaging and pricing (handled in product docs)\\n\\nh1. Principles\\n1. *Advisory by default.* Recommendations are read-only until explicit org-level opt-in is enabled.\\n2. *Safety over savings.* Any change must pass canary guardrails with automatic rollback.\\n3. *Explainability.* Each recommendation must include a rationale, expected savings range, and primary risk.\\n4. *Least-privilege & auditability.* Applying recommendations requires permissions and produces audit logs.\\n\\nh1. Inputs & Telemetry Requirements\\nEconomizer relies on aggregated telemetry, not raw prompts.\\n\\nh2. Required telemetry signals (aggregated)\\n* Request rate, concurrency, and queueing delay\\n* Token counts (prompt/completion), distribution summaries (p50/p95/p99)\\n* Prefix recurrence and estimated cache hit opportunity\\n* Model identifier, route identifier, and hardware class\\n* Latency (p50/p95/p99) and error rate\\n\\nh2. PII and retention requirements\\n* PII scrubbing is mandatory at collection time (no raw user text in Economizer pipelines).\\n* Aggregation windows:\\n  * Online summaries: 5-minute rollups\\n  * Offline scoring windows: 7 days by default\\n* Retention:\\n  * Aggregated Economizer summaries retained for *14 days* (updated from earlier 30-day guidance)\\n  * Audit logs retained per platform audit policy (see related pages)\\n\\nh2. Cardinality limits (required)\\nTo prevent high-cardinality explosions:\\n* Route-level keys must be normalized (no user IDs, no per-session keys).\\n* Prefix signatures use hashed buckets with a fixed cap per route per window.\\n* Any new telemetry dimension added to Economizer must include an explicit cardinality budget and a test demonstrating bounded growth.\\n\\nh1. Recommendation Types and Constraints\\nh2. Batching recommendations\\nEconomizer may propose:\\n* Target batch size range (min/target/max)\\n* Max queue delay (ms)\\n* Per-route concurrency caps where required to protect tail latency\\n\\nHard constraints:\\n* Recommendations must not increase p95 latency beyond the policy threshold in canary (see Guardrails).\\n* Routes marked as \\\"latency-critical\\\" (SLO tier 0) must use the stricter latency threshold.\\n\\nh2. Prefix cache recommendations\\nEconomizer may propose:\\n* Enable/disable prefix cache per route\\n* TTL range for cached prefixes\\n* Admission threshold based on observed recurrence (e.g., only cache prefixes above a recurrence score)\\n\\nHard constraints:\\n* Cache memory headroom must remain above the service minimum (see Guardrails).\\n* Any recommendation that increases cache footprint must include an eviction-risk note.\\n\\nh2. Quantization recommendations\\nEconomizer may propose:\\n* FP16 (baseline)\\n* INT8 (validated models only)\\n* FP8 (validated models and hardware only; added in 2026-05 standard update)\\n\\nConstraints and gates:\\n* Quantization recommendations are only surfaced if the Model Registry indicates the (model, quantization, hardware) combination is \\\"validated\\\".\\n* For models without validation, Economizer may suggest \\\"candidate\\\" quantization but it must be labeled *Requires QA* and cannot be auto-applied.\\n* A fallback profile must always be included (typically FP16) to enable safe rollback.\\n\\nh1. Scoring Policy (Cost vs Latency)\\nEconomizer ranks candidates using a utility score balancing cost savings and latency risk.\\n\\nh2. Default policy weights (2026-05)\\n* Cost savings weight: 1.0\\n* Latency penalty weight: 1.3 (increased from 1.0 to reduce tail-latency regressions observed in early beta)\\n* Error-rate penalty: hard fail if error-rate increases above guardrails\\n\\nNotes:\\n* The policy uses p99 latency as a primary risk signal for SLO tier 0 routes; p95 is the primary signal for other routes.\\n* Operators may tune sensitivity via approved configuration only. Any non-default weight set must be documented in the change ticket.\\n\\nh1. Guardrails and SLO Thresholds\\nThese guardrails are mandatory for any recommendation application.\\n\\nh2. Canary eligibility checks (pre-flight)\\nA route is eligible for canary if:\\n* It has at least 72 hours of stable telemetry in the last 7 days\\n* Baseline error rate is below 0.5% over the last 24 hours\\n* The route is not under active incident mitigation\\n\\nh2. Canary rollout guardrails (must pass)\\nGuardrails are evaluated against baseline for the same route.\\n\\nTable: Default guardrails\\n* SLO tier 0 routes:\\n  * p99 latency change: <= +2%\\n  * p95 latency change: <= +1%\\n  * error rate change: <= +0.1% absolute\\n* SLO tier 1+ routes:\\n  * p95 latency change: <= +3%\\n  * p99 latency change: <= +5%\\n  * error rate change: <= +0.2% absolute\\n\\nCache safety:\\n* Cache memory headroom must remain >= 15% during canary (updated from 10% to reduce eviction storms)\\n\\nAuto-rollback conditions:\\n* Any guardrail breach sustained for >= 10 minutes\\n* Any sudden error spike > 2x baseline for >= 5 minutes\\n\\nh2. Rollout stages (standard)\\n1. 1% traffic for 30\\u201360 minutes\\n2. 5% traffic for 60 minutes\\n3. 25% traffic for 2 hours\\n4. 100% if stable\\n\\nOperators may extend stages for high-risk changes (quantization, large cache expansions).\\n\\nh1. Operator Workflow (Console)\\nh2. Preview\\n1. Open *Console \\u2192 Economizer \\u2192 Recommendations*.\\n2. Filter by route, model, and time window.\\n3. Inspect each recommendation\\u2019s:\\n   * Expected savings range\\n   * Expected latency delta range\\n   * Primary risk factors\\n   * Compatibility notes (especially for quantization)\\n\\nh2. Simulation (required for quantization; recommended otherwise)\\nThe simulator replays anonymized trace summaries to estimate deltas.\\n\\nRequirements:\\n* Simulations must reference the same scoring window as the recommendation.\\n* If the simulator output diverges materially from the recommendation rationale, do not proceed; investigate telemetry quality.\\n\\nh2. Apply via canary\\n1. Select recommendation \\u2192 *Create Canary*.\\n2. Confirm rollback target (fallback profile must be set).\\n3. Start canary with default stages unless an exception is approved.\\n4. Monitor guardrails in the Rollouts dashboard.\\n5. Promote to 100% only after all stages pass.\\n\\nh2. Audit logging (required)\\nEvery applied recommendation must record:\\n* Actor (user/service)\\n* Route and model\\n* Before/after configuration\\n* Canary stage timestamps\\n* Rollback events (if any)\\n\\nh1. Operator Workflow (CLI Export)\\nCLI export is supported for audit and on-prem workflows.\\n\\nExample:\\nredwood-cli economizer export --route <route-id> --window 7d --format json --out recommendations.json\\n\\nRequirements:\\n* Exported artifacts must be stored in an approved audit location.\\n* Any manual application of exported recommendations must still follow the canary standard.\\n\\nh1. Expected Impact (Updated Guidance)\\nBased on internal benchmarks and production-like traces, typical savings are:\\n* 10\\u201330% token spend reduction for chat-heavy workloads when combining batching + prefix caching\\n* Additional savings from quantization vary widely and are gated by validation status\\n\\nLatency impact:\\n* With default policy weights, expected p95 impact is usually within +0% to +3% for eligible routes.\\n\\nThis guidance updates earlier internal claims of 15\\u201335% typical savings; the current range better reflects mixed workloads and stricter latency weights.\\n\\nh1. Known Limitations\\n* Cold-start routes with limited telemetry can receive noisy recommendations.\\n* Some proprietary or newly onboarded models may lack quantization validation metadata.\\n* Prefix cache recommendations are sensitive to prompt normalization; changes in templating can invalidate recurrence estimates.\\n\\nh1. Responsibilities\\n* Serving Runtime team: owns Economizer engine, scoring policy defaults, and rollout integration.\\n* SRE: owns telemetry retention, PII scrubbing enforcement, and observability requirements.\\n* Service owners: review recommendations, run canaries, and approve promotion to 100%.\\n\\nh1. Change Management\\nAny change to:\\n* Default policy weights\\n* Guardrail thresholds\\n* Telemetry retention or aggregation windows\\n\\nmust be documented as a standards update and reviewed by Serving Runtime + SRE.\\n\\nh1. References\\n* Economizer engine implementation: internal/economizer (repo: redwood)\\n* Rollout mechanism: standard canary rollout APIs and Console Rollouts dashboard\\n* Model Registry validation: Quantization compatibility matrix (see related pages)\\n\",\n  \"changelog\": \"2026-05-12: Updated retention to 14 days for aggregated summaries; raised cache headroom requirement to 15%; introduced FP8 as a gated/validated quantization option; increased default latency penalty weight to 1.3; updated expected savings guidance to 10\\u201330% typical.\\n2026-03-10: Initial published standard aligned with Economizer v1 rollout (batching, prefix cache, INT8 where validated), advisory-by-default posture, canary guardrails, and audit requirements.\",\n  \"source_context\": \"This Confluence standard supersedes earlier PR-level documentation for Economizer (introduced in redwood repo) by formalizing requirements, guardrails, and updated defaults based on beta learnings.\",\n  \"keywords\": [\n    \"Economizer\",\n    \"recommendations\",\n    \"batching\",\n    \"prefix cache\",\n    \"quantization\",\n    \"canary\",\n    \"rollout\",\n    \"guardrails\",\n    \"telemetry\",\n    \"cost optimization\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_noise_document\": true,\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"summary\",\n    \"body\",\n    \"changelog\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_79aba7601ab24ca699516975ecd5dd86\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Economizer Serving Recommendations Standard (Batching, Prefix Cache, Quantization)\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/performance-standards/economizer-serving-recommendations-standard.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: architecture-and-standards\n\nwhen combining batching + prefix caching * additional savings from quantization vary widely and are gated by validation status latency impact : * with default policy weights, expected p95 impact is usually within + 0 % to + 3 % for eligible routes. this guidance updates earlier internal claims of 15 – 35 % typical savings ; the current range better reflects mixed workloads and stricter latency weights. h1. known limitations * cold - start routes with limited telemetry can receive noisy recommendations. * some proprietary or newly onboarded models may lack quantization validation metadata. * prefix cache recommendations are sensitive to prompt normalization ; changes in templating can invalidate recurrence estimates.",

document.title: Economizer Serving Recommendations Standard (Batching, Prefix Cache, Quantization)
document.content:
{
  "title": "Economizer Serving Recommendations Standard (Batching, Prefix Cache, Quantization)",
  "space": "eng-serving-runtime",
  "author": "Priya Menon",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-03-10",
  "last_updated": "2026-05-12",
  "reviewers": [
    "Carlos Rivera",
    "Aisha Patel",
    "Evan Zhang",
    "Mina Al-Khalil"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "runtime",
    "performance",
    "cost",
    "ml-serving",
    "economizer",
    "standards",
    "rollouts"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "related_pages": [
    "confluence://eng-serving-runtime/rollouts/canary-rollout-standard",
    "confluence://eng-sre/observability/telemetry-retention-and-pii-scrubbing",
    "confluence://eng-serving-runtime/caching/prefix-cache-architecture",
    "confluence://eng-serving-runtime/model-registry/quantization-compatibility-matrix"
  ],
  "summary": "This standard defines how Redwood Inference uses Economizer to generate, review, and safely apply automated serving recommendations for batching, prefix caching, and quantization on a per-route and per-model basis. It establishes required guardrails (SLO impact thresholds, rollback, audit logging), telemetry requirements, and the operator workflow in Console/CLI.",
  "body": "h1. Overview
Economizer is Redwood Inference’s recommendation engine for serving configuration changes. It analyzes historical request traces plus live telemetry summaries to propose per-route and per-model adjustments that reduce token spend while keeping latency and error-rate within policy.

Economizer produces three classes of recommendations:
* *Batching* (e.g., target batch size range, max queue delay)
* *Prefix caching* (e.g., enablement, TTL and admission thresholds)
* *Quantization profiles* (e.g., FP16 baseline to INT8/FP8 where validated)

This page is the canonical standard for how recommendations are generated, surfaced, validated, and applied.

h1. Scope
This standard applies to:
* All production serving routes in Redwood Inference clusters
* Console-based recommendation preview and canary application flows
* CLI export used for audit/on-prem workflows

Out of scope:
* Model quality evaluation methodology beyond the defined quantization gates (see related pages)
* Customer-facing product messaging and pricing (handled in product docs)

h1. Principles
1. *Advisory by default.* Recommendations are read-only until explicit org-level opt-in is enabled.
2. *Safety over savings.* Any change must pass canary guardrails with automatic rollback.
3. *Explainability.* Each recommendation must include a rationale, expected savings range, and primary risk.
4. *Least-privilege & auditability.* Applying recommendations requires permissions and produces audit logs.

h1. Inputs & Telemetry Requirements
Economizer relies on aggregated telemetry, not raw prompts.

h2. Required telemetry signals (aggregated)
* Request rate, concurrency, and queueing delay
* Token counts (prompt/completion), distribution summaries (p50/p95/p99)
* Prefix recurrence and estimated cache hit opportunity
* Model identifier, route identifier, and hardware class
* Latency (p50/p95/p99) and error rate

h2. PII and retention requirements
* PII scrubbing is mandatory at collection time (no raw user text in Economizer pipelines).
* Aggregation windows:
  * Online summaries: 5-minute rollups
  * Offline scoring windows: 7 days by default
* Retention:
  * Aggregated Economizer summaries retained for *14 days* (updated from earlier 30-day guidance)
  * Audit logs retained per platform audit policy (see related pages)

h2. Cardinality limits (required)
To prevent high-cardinality explosions:
* Route-level keys must be normalized (no user IDs, no per-session keys).
* Prefix signatures use hashed buckets with a fixed cap per route per window.
* Any new telemetry dimension added to Economizer must include an explicit cardinality budget and a test demonstrating bounded growth.

h1. Recommendation Types and Constraints
h2. Batching recommendations
Economizer may propose:
* Target batch size range (min/target/max)
* Max queue delay (ms)
* Per-route concurrency caps where required to protect tail latency

Hard constraints:
* Recommendations must not increase p95 latency beyond the policy threshold in canary (see Guardrails).
* Routes marked as "latency-critical" (SLO tier 0) must use the stricter latency threshold.

h2. Prefix cache recommendations
Economizer may propose:
* Enable/disable prefix cache per route
* TTL range for cached prefixes
* Admission threshold based on observed recurrence (e.g., only cache prefixes above a recurrence score)

Hard constraints:
* Cache memory headroom must remain above the service minimum (see Guardrails).
* Any recommendation that increases cache footprint must include an eviction-risk note.

h2. Quantization recommendations
Economizer may propose:
* FP16 (baseline)
* INT8 (validated models only)
* FP8 (validated models and hardware only; added in 2026-05 standard update)

Constraints and gates:
* Quantization recommendations are only surfaced if the Model Registry indicates the (model, quantization, hardware) combination is "validated".
* For models without validation, Economizer may suggest "candidate" quantization but it must be labeled *Requires QA* and cannot be auto-applied.
* A fallback profile must always be included (typically FP16) to enable safe rollback.

h1. Scoring Policy (Cost vs Latency)
Economizer ranks candidates using a utility score balancing cost savings and latency risk.

h2. Default policy weights (2026-05)
* Cost savings weight: 1.0
* Latency penalty weight: 1.3 (increased from 1.0 to reduce tail-latency regressions observed in early beta)
* Error-rate penalty: hard fail if error-rate increases above guardrails

Notes:
* The policy uses p99 latency as a primary risk signal for SLO tier 0 routes; p95 is the primary signal for other routes.
* Operators may tune sensitivity via approved configuration only. Any non-default weight set must be documented in the change ticket.

h1. Guardrails and SLO Thresholds
These guardrails are mandatory for any recommendation application.

h2. Canary eligibility checks (pre-flight)
A route is eligible for canary if:
* It has at least 72 hours of stable telemetry in the last 7 days
* Baseline error rate is below 0.5% over the last 24 hours
* The route is not under active incident mitigation

h2. Canary rollout guardrails (must pass)
Guardrails are evaluated against baseline for the same route.

Table: Default guardrails
* SLO tier 0 routes:
  * p99 latency change: <= +2%
  * p95 latency change: <= +1%
  * error rate change: <= +0.1% absolute
* SLO tier 1+ routes:
  * p95 latency change: <= +3%
  * p99 latency change: <= +5%
  * error rate change: <= +0.2% absolute

Cache safety:
* Cache memory headroom must remain >= 15% during canary (updated from 10% to reduce eviction storms)

Auto-rollback conditions:
* Any guardrail breach sustained for >= 10 minutes
* Any sudden error spike > 2x baseline for >= 5 minutes

h2. Rollout stages (standard)
1. 1% traffic for 30–60 minutes
2. 5% traffic for 60 minutes
3. 25% traffic for 2 hours
4. 100% if stable

Operators may extend stages for high-risk changes (quantization, large cache expansions).

h1. Operator Workflow (Console)
h2. Preview
1. Open *Console → Economizer → Recommendations*.
2. Filter by route, model, and time window.
3. Inspect each recommendation’s:
   * Expected savings range
   * Expected latency delta range
   * Primary risk factors
   * Compatibility notes (especially for quantization)

h2. Simulation (required for quantization; recommended otherwise)
The simulator replays anonymized trace summaries to estimate deltas.

Requirements:
* Simulations must reference the same scoring window as the recommendation.
* If the simulator output diverges materially from the recommendation rationale, do not proceed; investigate telemetry quality.

h2. Apply via canary
1. Select recommendation → *Create Canary*.
2. Confirm rollback target (fallback profile must be set).
3. Start canary with default stages unless an exception is approved.
4. Monitor guardrails in the Rollouts dashboard.
5. Promote to 100% only after all stages pass.

h2. Audit logging (required)
Every applied recommendation must record:
* Actor (user/service)
* Route and model
* Before/after configuration
* Canary stage timestamps
* Rollback events (if any)

h1. Operator Workflow (CLI Export)
CLI export is supported for audit and on-prem workflows.

Example:
redwood-cli economizer export --route <route-id> --window 7d --format json --out recommendations.json

Requirements:
* Exported artifacts must be stored in an approved audit location.
* Any manual application of exported recommendations must still follow the canary standard.

h1. Expected Impact (Updated Guidance)
Based on internal benchmarks and production-like traces, typical savings are:
* 10–30% token spend reduction for chat-heavy workloads when combining batching + prefix caching
* Additional savings from quantization vary widely and are gated by validation status

Latency impact:
* With default policy weights, expected p95 impact is usually within +0% to +3% for eligible routes.

This guidance updates earlier internal claims of 15–35% typical savings; the current range better reflects mixed workloads and stricter latency weights.

h1. Known Limitations
* Cold-start routes with limited telemetry can receive noisy recommendations.
* Some proprietary or newly onboarded models may lack quantization validation metadata.
* Prefix cache recommendations are sensitive to prompt normalization; changes in templating can invalidate recurrence estimates.

h1. Responsibilities
* Serving Runtime team: owns Economizer engine, scoring policy defaults, and rollout integration.
* SRE: owns telemetry retention, PII scrubbing enforcement, and observability requirements.
* Service owners: review recommendations, run canaries, and approve promotion to 100%.

h1. Change Management
Any change to:
* Default policy weights
* Guardrail thresholds
* Telemetry retention or aggregation windows

must be documented as a standards update and reviewed by Serving Runtime + SRE.

h1. References
* Economizer engine implementation: internal/economizer (repo: redwood)
* Rollout mechanism: standard canary rollout APIs and Console Rollouts dashboard
* Model Registry validation: Quantization compatibility matrix (see related pages)
",
  "changelog": "2026-05-12: Updated retention to 14 days for aggregated summaries; raised cache headroom requirement to 15%; introduced FP8 as a gated/validated quantization option; increased default latency penalty weight to 1.3; updated expected savings guidance to 10–30% typical.
2026-03-10: Initial published standard aligned with Economizer v1 rollout (batching, prefix cache, INT8 where validated), advisory-by-default posture, canary guardrails, and audit requirements.",
  "source_context": "This Confluence standard supersedes earlier PR-level documentation for Economizer (introduced in redwood repo) by formalizing requirements, guardrails, and updated defaults based on beta learnings.",
  "keywords": [
    "Economizer",
    "recommendations",
    "batching",
    "prefix cache",
    "quantization",
    "canary",
    "rollout",
    "guardrails",
    "telemetry",
    "cost optimization"
  ],
  "dataset_noise_document": true,
  "title_field_name": "title",
  "content_field_names": [
    "summary",
    "body",
    "changelog"
  ],

# Agent Instructions for vLLM

> These instructions apply to **all** AI-assisted contributions to `vllm-project/vllm`.
> Breaching these guidelines can result in automatic banning.

## 1. Contribution Policy (Mandatory)

### Duplicate-work checks

Before proposing a PR, run these checks:

```bash
gh issue view <issue_number> --repo vllm-project/vllm --comments
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "<issue_number> in:body"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "<short area keywords>"
```

- If an open PR already addresses the same fix, do not open another.
- If your approach is materially different, explain the difference in the issue.

### No low-value busywork PRs

Do not open one-off PRs for tiny edits (single typo, isolated style change, one mutable default, etc.). Mechanical cleanups are acceptable only when bundled with substantive work.

### Accountability

- Pure code-agent PRs are **not allowed**. A human submitter must understand and defend the change end-to-end.
- The submitting human must review every changed line and run relevant tests.
- PR descriptions for AI-assisted work **must** include:
    - Why this is not duplicating an existing PR.
    - Test commands run and results.
    - Model evaluation results when the change affects output, accuracy, or serving.
    - Clear statement that AI assistance was used.

### Fail-closed behavior

If work is duplicate/trivial busywork, **do not proceed**. Return a short explanation of what is missing.

---

## 2. Development Workflow

- **Never use system `python3` or bare `pip`/`pip install`.** All Python commands must go through `uv` and `.venv/bin/python`.

### Environment setup

```bash
# Install `uv` if you don't have it already:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# Always use `uv` for Python environment management:
uv venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

# Always make sure `pre-commit` and its hooks are installed:
uv pip install -r requirements/lint.txt
pre-commit install
```

### Installing dependencies

```bash
# If you are only making Python changes:
VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 uv pip install -e . --torch-backend=auto

# If you are also making C/C++ changes:
uv pip install -e . --torch-backend=auto
```

### Tests

> Requires [Environment setup](#environment-setup) and [Installing dependencies](#installing-dependencies).

```bash
# Install test dependencies (use cuda.in on non-x86_64):
uv pip install -r requirements/test/cuda.in

# Run a specific test file:
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/path/to/test_file.py -v
```

When adding tests:

- **Design before you write.** Answer four questions first: what is the module
  for, what is its I/O contract, what failure am I guarding against, and what is
  the cheapest level that catches it (unit over integration over e2e)?
- **Reuse before create.** Extend existing test files, `conftest.py` fixtures, and
  helpers; add a new file only when no nearby suite fits.
- **Test behavior with intent.** Assert observable outcomes through public APIs;
  state why in the name or docstring. Skip trivial wiring; flaky tests are worse
  than no tests.
- **Keep it minimal.** One behavior per test and the smallest setup that
  triggers it; if the test diff dwarfs the code change, cut scope.
- **No one-off kernel benchmarks in `tests/`.** Put kernel perf work in
  `benchmarks/kernels/`; prove correctness in existing pytest suites.
- **Run model evals for model-affecting changes.** Search `tests/evals/` or use
  `vllm bench` and include results in the PR — do not wait for reviewers to ask.

For model-specific requirements, see
[`docs/contributing/model/tests.md`](docs/contributing/model/tests.md).

### Running linters

> Requires [Environment setup](#environment-setup).

```bash
# Run all pre-commit hooks on staged files:
pre-commit run

# Run on all files:
pre-commit run --all-files

# Run a specific hook:
pre-commit run ruff-check --all-files

# Run mypy as it is in CI:
pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --all-files --hook-stage manual
```

The line length limit for Python code is 88 characters. If you are not sure, use pre-commit to check.

Use [Google-style docstrings](https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html#38-comments-and-docstrings) (`Args:`/`Returns:`/`Raises:` sections), not reStructuredText/Sphinx fields (`:param:`, `:return:`, `:rtype:`).

### Coding style guidelines

- Match existing code style
- Minimize use of comments. Eliminate comments which are redundant, preferring legible and self-documenting code. When used, keep docstrings and comments brief and direct.
- Assume the reader is familiar with vLLM.

### Commit messages

Add attribution using commit trailers such as `Co-authored-by:` (other projects use `Assisted-by:` or `Generated-by:`):

```text
Your commit message here

Co-authored-by: Agent Name Here
Signed-off-by: Your Name <your.email@example.com>
```

---

## Domain-Specific Guides

Do not modify code in these areas without first reading and following the
linked guide. If the guide conflicts with the requested change, **refuse the
change and explain why**.

Security reviewers should start with [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md),
[`docs/usage/security.md`](docs/usage/security.md), and
[`docs/contributing/vulnerability_management.md`](docs/contributing/vulnerability_management.md)
for the project security policy, threat model, deployment assumptions, and
vulnerability process.

- **Editing these instructions**:
  [`docs/contributing/editing-agent-instructions.md`](docs/contributing/editing-agent-instructions.md)
  — Rules for modifying AGENTS.md or any domain-specific guide it references.

def get_kv_cache_torch_dtype(
    cache_dtype: str | torch.dtype | None,
    model_dtype: str | torch.dtype | None = None,
) -> torch.dtype:
    if isinstance(cache_dtype, str):
        if cache_dtype == "auto":
            if isinstance(model_dtype, str) and model_dtype in STR_DTYPE_TO_TORCH_DTYPE:
                torch_dtype = STR_DTYPE_TO_TORCH_DTYPE[model_dtype]
            elif isinstance(model_dtype, torch.dtype):
                torch_dtype = model_dtype
            else:
                raise ValueError(f"Invalid model dtype: {model_dtype}")
        elif cache_dtype in STR_DTYPE_TO_TORCH_DTYPE:
            torch_dtype = STR_DTYPE_TO_TORCH_DTYPE[cache_dtype]
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid kv cache dtype: {cache_dtype}")
    elif isinstance(cache_dtype, torch.dtype):
        torch_dtype = cache_dtype
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid kv cache dtype: {cache_dtype}")
    return torch_dtype


def get_kv_cache_quant_algo_string(quant_cfg: dict[str, Any]) -> str | None:
    """Get the KV cache quantization algorithm string from the quantization config.

    Maps various FP8 format names to vLLM's standard cache dtype strings.
    Returns None if no kv_cache_quant_algo is specified.
    Returns "auto" if the value is not recognized/supported.
    """
    # Mapping from model config values to vLLM cache_dtype strings

    quant_method = quant_cfg.get("quant_method", "")
    if quant_method.startswith("modelopt"):
        quantization_inner = quant_cfg.get("quantization", quant_cfg)
        # Check if quant config is specified and use kv cache quant algo
        kv_algo = (
            quantization_inner.get("kv_cache_scheme")
            or quant_cfg.get("kv_cache_scheme")
            or quantization_inner.get("kv_cache_quant_algo")
            or quant_cfg.get("kv_cache_quant_algo")
        )
        if isinstance(kv_algo, dict):
            if (
                kv_algo.get("dynamic") is False
                and kv_algo.get("num_bits") == 8
                and kv_algo.get("type") == "float"
            ):
                kv_algo = "fp8"
            elif kv_algo.get("num_bits") == 4 and kv_algo.get("type") == "float":
                kv_algo = "nvfp4"
            else:
                # Unknown/unsupported format - return "auto" as safe fallback
                logger.warning(
                    "WARNING: Unknown kv_cache_quant_algo '%s' in model "
                    "config. Supported values: %s. Falling back to 'auto'.",
                    f"{kv_algo}",
                    list(MODELOPT_TO_VLLM_KV_CACHE_DTYPE_MAP.keys()),
                )
                return "auto"
        if isinstance(kv_algo, str):
            kv_algo_lower = kv_algo.lower()

            # Try to map to vLLM's standard format
            if kv_algo_lower in MODELOPT_TO_VLLM_KV_CACHE_DTYPE_MAP:
                return MODELOPT_TO_VLLM_KV_CACHE_DTYPE_MAP[kv_algo_lower]
            else:
                # Unknown/unsupported format - return "auto" as safe fallback
                logger.warning(
                    "WARNING: Unknown kv_cache_quant_algo '%s' in model "
                    "config. Supported values: %s. Falling back to 'auto'.",
                    kv_algo,
                    list(MODELOPT_TO_VLLM_KV_CACHE_DTYPE_MAP.keys()),
                )
                return "auto"
    return None


def get_kv_cache_quant_algo_dtype(quant_cfg: dict[str, Any]) -> torch.dtype | None:
    """Get the KV cache quantization algorithm dtype from the quantization config."""
    kv_algo_str = get_kv_cache_quant_algo_string(quant_cfg)
    if kv_algo_str is not None and kv_algo_str != "auto":
        # Only convert if we have a valid dtype string (not "auto" fallback)
        return STR_DTYPE_TO_TORCH_DTYPE[kv_algo_str]
    return None


def resolve_kv_cache_dtype_string(
    kv_cache_dtype: str, model_config: ModelConfig
) -> str:
    """Resolve 'auto' kv_cache_dtype to the actual string value from model config.
    Returns the resolved cache_dtype string.
    """
    if kv_cache_dtype != "auto":
        return kv_cache_dtype

    hf_cfg = getattr(model_config, "hf_config", None)

  "title": "Private VPC: narrow-window version pinning & rollback cadence",
  "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Private VPC: narrow-window version pinning & rollback cadence\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/gmail\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/gmail/neha_kapoor/20260712-vpc-narrow-window-pin-cadence.json\nConnector: gmail\nWorkspace: neha_kapoor\n\n- kv cache warm - up : 15m per canary is fine, but cold - starts for quantized kernels can add ~ 30 - 90s per model shard. we ' ll need to ensure the canary covers the heaviest shard and that the cache is pre - populated with a representative prefix set. - pin semantics : pin at the deployment unit ( pool ) rather than binary - level to avoid inconsistent kernel selection. we should capture the model hash + quantization profile in the audit event. - rollback automation : i propose a two - step rollback script : 1 ) atomic pin swap + immediate traffic redirect to previous pool, 2 ) kv flush to avoid stale state. the script is in proj - 1234 ( https : / / jira. redwood. com / browse / proj - 1234",

  "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Private upgrade operator for data-plane zero-impact switchover\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-17711-private-upgrade-operator-safe-switchover.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: Private Deployments\nTeam: engineering\n\n- operator design : state machine with phases : precheck - > canary - > validate - > rolling - > finish. each phase has timeout and retry budget. - canary strategy : start 1 replica with traffic sampled ( 1 - 2 % ) using envoy weighted routing or service mesh header. use request shadowing for acceptance tests. - kv cache migration : prefer in - place kv warming using background prefill jobs ; avoid flushing unless safe. add cache version header to detect stale entries. - traffic shift : use gradual weight shifts with safety gates ( metric checks every 30s ). implement circuit - breaker that aborts and triggers rollback if thresholds crossed. - rollback : three - step rollback that stops new deployments, shifts traffic back to previous version with priority weighting, drains new pods, and optionally",

  "title": "Private deployment upgrade plan: version pinning, maintenance window & rollback",
  "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Private deployment upgrade plan: version pinning, maintenance window & rollback\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/gmail\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/gmail/lauren_bishop/20260310-private-upgrade-maintenance-plan.json\nConnector: gmail\nWorkspace: lauren_bishop\n\nwill run during the deployment ; we recommend routing 5 % traffic to canary nodes for 30 minutes to collect kv warm state. operational checklist ( abbreviated ) : 1 ) pre - checks : snapshot kv store, create backup of deployments, export metrics baseline ( latency / cost / throughput ). 2 ) canary : deploy to 2 nodes in a separate subnet, run smoke tests ( healthcheck endpoints + sample prompts ), validate quantization artifacts. 3 ) roll forward : rolling update across azs with traffic draining and 10 - minute pause per availability zone. 4 ) post - checks : run full acceptance test set, confirm no regressions in quality ( eval set pass ), confirm cost delta within 5 %. 5 ) rollback : helm rollback, restart previous pods, restore kv snapshot if cache corruption found",

import pytest
import torch

from vllm.utils.torch_utils import (

    current_stream,

)


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    ("src_dtype", "tgt_dtype", "expected_result"),
    [
        # Different precision_levels
        (torch.bool, torch.int8, True),
        (torch.bool, torch.float16, True),
        (torch.bool, torch.complex32, True),
        (torch.int64, torch.bool, False),
        (torch.int64, torch.float16, True),
        (torch.int64, torch.complex32, True),
        (torch.float64, torch.bool, False),
        (torch.float64, torch.int8, False),
        (torch.float64, torch.complex32, True),
        (torch.complex128, torch.bool, False),
        (torch.complex128, torch.int8, False),
        (torch.complex128, torch.float16, False),
        # precision_level=0
        (torch.bool, torch.bool, True),
        # precision_level=1
        (torch.int8, torch.int16, True),
        (torch.int16, torch.int8, False),
        (torch.uint8, torch.int8, False),
        (torch.int8, torch.uint8, False),
        # precision_level=2
        (torch.float16, torch.float32, True),
        (torch.float32, torch.float16, False),
        (torch.bfloat16, torch.float32, True),
        (torch.float32, torch.bfloat16, False),
        # precision_level=3
        (torch.complex32, torch.complex64, True),
        (torch.complex64, torch.complex32, False),
    ],
)
def test_is_lossless_cast(src_dtype, tgt_dtype, expected_result):
    assert is_lossless_cast(src_dtype, tgt_dtype) == expected_result


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    ("dtypes", "expected_result"),
    [
        ([torch.bool], torch.bool),
        ([torch.bool, torch.int8], torch.int8),
        ([torch.bool, torch.int8, torch.float16], torch.float16),
        ([torch.bool, torch.int8, torch.float16, torch.complex32], torch.complex32),  # noqa: E501
    ],
)
def test_common_broadcastable_dtype(dtypes, expected_result):
    assert common_broadcastable_dtype(dtypes) == expected_result


def _test_stream_thread(main_expected_stream: torch.cuda.Stream):
    import threading

    child_stream = torch.cuda.Stream()
    thread_stream_ready = threading.Event()
    thread_can_exit = threading.Event()

    def child_thread_func():
        with torch.cuda.stream(child_stream):
            thread_stream_ready.set()
            thread_can_exit.wait(timeout=10)

    child_thread = threading.Thread(target=child_thread_func)
    child_thread.start()

    try:
        assert thread_stream_ready.wait(timeout=5), (
            "Child thread failed to enter stream context in time"
        )

        main_current_stream = current_stream()

        assert main_current_stream != child_stream, (
            "Main thread's current_stream was contaminated by child thread"
        )
        assert main_current_stream == main_expected_stream, (
            f"Main thread's stream changed unexpectedly. "
            f"Expected {main_expected_stream}, got {main_current_stream}"
        )

        thread_can_exit.set()

    finally:
        child_thread.join(timeout=5)
        if child_thread.is_alive():
            pytest.fail("Child thread failed to exit properly")


def test_current_stream_multithread():
    if not torch.cuda.is_available():
        pytest.skip("CUDA not available")

    main_dedicated_stream = current_stream()

    assert main_dedicated_stream.cuda_stream != 0, (
        "ROCm/CUDA should create a dedicated stream, not use default stream (0x0)"
    )

    main_stream_again = current_stream()
    assert main_stream_again == main_dedicated_stream, (
        "Multiple calls to current_stream should return the same dedicated stream"
    )

    _test_stream_thread(main_dedicated_stream)

Resolved and published vLLM issue #34752 to `person/jamal-pierce`.

Precedence rule:

- Supported checkpoint `kv_cache_quant_algo` is authoritative.
- Omitted dtype and explicit `auto` adopt checkpoint metadata.
- Equivalent explicit values such as `fp8`/`fp8_e4m3` are accepted.
- Conflicting overrides fail during configuration with corrective guidance.
- Unsupported checkpoint metadata also fails early.
- Without metadata, `auto` follows model dtype; explicit supported values win.
